prompt: The shop creates a public hosted zone for `shop.example.com` and writes its records. Nobody on the internet gets an answer from it. What is missing?
hint: Who sends the askers to the zone?

choices.text: A private zone of the same name, associated with the VPC
choices.why: A private zone answers inside a VPC and nowhere else. It adds nothing for a stranger on the internet.

choices.text: The delegation at the registrar
choices.why: Right. Until the parent domain's NS records name Route 53's servers, no resolver is ever sent to the zone.

choices.text: A region, since `env.sh` names `sa-east-1` and the zone has none
choices.why: Route 53 is global; a zone never has a region, and that is not why nobody is answered.

choices.text: An SOA record, which every public zone has to be given by hand after it is created
choices.why: The SOA and the NS records are created with the zone, as the listing showed.

prompt: A machine in the shop's VPC asks for `db.shop.internal`, which lives in a private zone. Which part of AWS answers it?
hint: The address it asks is inside the VPC.

choices.text: One of the four name servers in the zone's delegation set
choices.why: Those serve public zones to the internet. A private zone is not delegated anywhere.

choices.text: The registrar, which keeps a copy of every zone
choices.why: A registrar keeps the delegation of a domain, not its records, and knows nothing of a private zone.

choices.text: The Route 53 Resolver at the VPC's base address plus two
choices.why: Right: `10.20.0.2` for this VPC. It answers from the associated private zones first, while DNS support and hostnames are on.

choices.text: Any resolver on the internet, once the zone is associated
choices.why: Association makes the zone visible to that VPC only; to the internet it does not exist.

prompt: To clean up, a colleague deletes the shop's public zone and creates a new one with the same records. The site stops resolving everywhere. Why?
hint: What did the registrar write down: a zone, or servers?

choices.text: The records were copied without their TTLs
choices.why: A missing TTL would be refused by the batch; it would not make a correct zone unreachable.

choices.text: A new zone takes two days to become `INSYNC`
choices.why: Changes reach Route 53's servers in about a minute. Two days is the TTL of the parent's NS records, and they still name the old servers.

choices.text: The new zone has a new set of name servers, and `.com` still delegates to the old ones
choices.why: Right. The delegation names servers, and the set is chosen when a zone is created. The registrar has to be given the new four.

choices.text: Deleting a zone also deletes the domain at the registrar
choices.why: The registration is untouched; it simply points at servers that no longer answer for anything.

prompt: At the list of 11 September 2026, what does the shop pay a month for 30 hosted zones, before any query?
hint: The first 25 have one price, the rest another.

prompt: A deployment script retries `create-hosted-zone` after a timeout, with the same `--caller-reference`. What does AWS do with the retry?
hint: What is the reference for?

choices.text: Creates a second zone, exactly as moto did in the lab
choices.why: That is moto's behaviour, and the section says moto does not keep this promise.

choices.text: Refuses it with `HostedZoneAlreadyExists`
choices.why: Right. The caller reference exists so a retry cannot leave two zones of the same name.

choices.text: Replaces the first zone, keeping its name servers
choices.why: Route 53 never replaces a zone on a create. It either makes one or refuses.

choices.text: Merges the two requests into one change and answers `PENDING`
choices.why: A change batch is about records. A zone is created once, or the second attempt is refused.

prompt: A batch holds five `CREATE` actions, and the third names a record that already exists. What does Route 53 do?
hint: A batch is one unit.

choices.text: Applies the first two and stops at the third
choices.why: That would leave the zone half changed, which is exactly what a batch exists to prevent.

choices.text: Applies the four that can be applied and reports the third
choices.why: Route 53 never applies part of a batch. The four valid ones wait with the failed one.

choices.text: Applies none of them and answers `InvalidChangeBatch`
choices.why: Right. The batch is applied whole or not at all, and the error names the record that stopped it.

choices.text: Turns the third into an `UPSERT` and applies all five
choices.why: Route 53 does what the batch says. Choosing `UPSERT` is the author's decision, not the service's.

prompt: The shop wants `shop.example.com`, with nothing in front, to lead to its load balancer. Why is an alias record the answer and a `CNAME` is not?
hint: What else lives at the apex?

choices.text: A `CNAME` must be alone at its name, and the apex holds NS and SOA
choices.why: Right. An alias is an ordinary `A` record to the asker, so it sits beside the NS, the SOA and the MX.

choices.text: A `CNAME` cannot point at a name outside its own zone, and the load balancer's name lives in AWS's
choices.why: It can; that is what a `CNAME` is mostly for. The rule that matters is about the apex.

choices.text: A load balancer's name changes every hour, and only an alias follows it
choices.why: The name is stable; its addresses are what move, and a `CNAME` would follow those too. The trouble is where the record sits.

choices.text: A `CNAME` is a type moto does not store
choices.why: moto stored `www` as a `CNAME`, and even stored one at the apex, which AWS refuses.

prompt: In moto, `get-change` answered `INSYNC` for `/change/NOSUCHCHANGE`. What should you conclude?
hint: Was there ever such a change?

choices.text: The change was applied before moto restarted
choices.why: There was never a change with that id. moto answers the same for any id at all.

choices.text: Nothing about the zone: moto answers that for any id
choices.why: Right. In moto, the zone's own listing is the evidence; `get-change` only shows the shape of the answer.

choices.text: That AWS also skips the `PENDING` state for small changes
choices.why: AWS answers `PENDING` until every name server has the change. moto's answer says nothing about AWS.

prompt: Match each record type to what it answers with.
hint: Five types from the shop's first batch, and one answer left over.

pairs.right: the domain's mail server, with a preference
free text, such as an SPF policy
another name to look up instead

prompt: A record carries a TTL of 86,400. Five minutes after it is changed, a customer still reaches the old address. Where is the old answer coming from?
hint: Nothing is pushed anywhere.

choices.text: From Route 53 servers that have not yet received the change
choices.why: Those have it within about a minute. Five minutes on, they all answer with the new address.

choices.text: From the registrar, which still holds the old record
choices.why: A registrar holds the delegation, not the zone's records.

choices.text: From a resolver's cache, kept for up to a day
choices.why: Right. The resolver was promised 86,400 seconds, and it keeps that promise. Lowering the TTL a day before is the fix.

choices.text: From moto, which serves DNS on port 4567
choices.why: moto serves no DNS at all. And a customer on the internet would never reach it.

prompt: Put the steps of moving `www` to a new address with the least delay in order.
hint: The caches have to be holding the short TTL before the change.
items: lower the record's TTL to 60 seconds
change the record to the new address
raise the TTL again once the new address has proved itself
trap: Changing the address before waiting is the usual slip: the caches that asked before the TTL was lowered still hold the old answer for the old, long TTL.

prompt: The API's primary record carries a health check. While the check reports unhealthy, what does Route 53 answer for `api.shop.example.com`?
hint: A failover pair has two halves.

choices.text: Nothing, until the primary is healthy again
choices.why: That is what the secondary exists to prevent.

choices.text: Both addresses, and the client picks one
choices.why: Returning several healthy values is multivalue. Failover gives one record, the primary or the secondary.

choices.text: The secondary, `198.51.100.20` in Virginia, until the primary's check passes again
choices.why: Right. The primary is left out while its check is unhealthy, and the secondary, with no check of its own, is always considered healthy.

choices.text: The primary, since Route 53 sits in the path and reroutes the packets
choices.why: Route 53 never touches the traffic. It chooses an answer, and the answer is the secondary.

prompt: A streaming licence allows a catalogue only to viewers in Brazil. Which routing policy fits?
hint: A law cares where the person is, not how fast the network is.

choices.text: Latency, so Brazilians reach São Paulo first
choices.why: Latency follows the network, and a viewer in Uruguay may well have the lowest latency to São Paulo too.

choices.text: Weighted, with all the weight on São Paulo
choices.why: A weight is the same for every asker. It cannot tell one country from another.

choices.text: Geoproximity, with a large bias towards São Paulo
choices.why: Geoproximity draws a boundary by distance, and a border is not a distance.

choices.text: Geolocation by country, with a `Default` record
choices.why: Right. It chooses by where the asker is, which is what a licence is about, and the `Default` answers the rest of the world.

prompt: Records that share a name under one routing policy are told apart by their `___`.
hint: The field that held `current`, `canary`, `sao-paulo` and `virginia`.

prompt: A name has three weighted records with weights 6, 3 and 1. What share of the answers, in per cent, does the record weighted 3 get?
hint: A weight divided by the sum of the weights.

prompt: In moto, `get-health-check-status` reports `Success: HTTP Status Code: 200` for a check of `203.0.113.20`. A colleague takes that as proof the failover works. What is wrong with that?
hint: Did anything travel to that address?

choices.text: Nothing: moto probes the address once, from `us-east-1`, and one success is enough for a check of this kind
choices.why: moto probes nothing. The region and the code in its answer are the same for every check.

choices.text: Only that the status needs three successes before it counts
choices.why: The threshold is about real probes, and here there were none at all.

choices.text: moto sent no probe; it says that of every check
choices.why: Right. moto can confirm the records and the check are wired together; whether the switch happens is AWS's to show, not the lab's.

choices.text: The check is HTTPS, and moto only probes plain HTTP
choices.why: moto probes neither. The protocol makes no difference to an answer it invents.

prompt: Which of these, at the list of 11 September 2026, cost nothing? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two lines of the table are free, under conditions.

choices.text: Queries answered from an alias to a load balancer
choices.why: Right. `Intra-AWS-DNS-Queries` is priced at zero.

choices.text: Queries answered from a `CNAME` to a load balancer
choices.why: A `CNAME` is an ordinary record, billed at 0.40 a million. Only the alias is free.

choices.text: The first 50 health checks of AWS endpoints
choices.why: Right. `Health-Check-AWS` is free up to 50, then 0.50 a month each.

choices.text: A health check of `203.0.113.20`
choices.why: That address is outside AWS, so it is the 0.75 line, plus 2.00 for HTTPS.

choices.text: The first million geolocation queries of a month
choices.why: Geolocation queries are 0.70 a million from the first one.

prompt: `aws route53 test-dns-answer` answers `404 Not Found` in the lab. What does that tell you about the record?
hint: Who answered the 404?

choices.text: That the weighted records were never written
choices.why: The listing just above printed them. The 404 is about the command, not the records.

choices.text: Nothing: moto 5.2.3 does not implement the command
choices.why: Right. Against AWS the command answers with the values Route 53 would return; in moto it is not there.

choices.text: That Route 53 has no answer for `search.shop.example.com`
choices.why: A missing name would come back as an answer about the name. This is moto saying it has no such operation.

choices.text: That the zone is private and cannot be tested
choices.why: The zone asked about is the public one, and the 404 would be the same for either.

prompt: The shop moves its API from São Paulo to Virginia with a failover pair, TTL 60. Customers report the old address for an hour after the switch. Which explanation fits the lesson?
hint: Sixty seconds is a promise; who might not keep it?

choices.text: Route 53 takes an hour to notice that a health check has turned unhealthy and to stop giving the primary
choices.why: With a 30-second interval and three failures, the verdict comes in about a minute and a half.

choices.text: A cache on the way kept the answer past its TTL
choices.why: Right. The TTL is the floor on a failover's speed, and only as good as the caches that honour it; some clients and resolvers keep answers longer.

choices.text: The secondary had no health check, so Route 53 refused to use it
choices.why: A record with no check is always considered healthy, which is why the secondary was given at all.

choices.text: The change batch was still `PENDING`
choices.why: A failover needs no batch: both records already exist, and the health check decides between them.

prompt: Put the steps a resolver takes to find `mail.shop.example.com` in order, starting with an empty cache.
hint: From the top of the tree to the zone.
items: ask a root server, which refers it to `.com`
ask a `.com` server, which refers it to Route 53's four name servers
ask `ns-2048.awsdns-64.com`, which answers from the hosted zone
keep the answer for the record's TTL
trap: Starting at Route 53 is the usual slip: the resolver only learns of those servers from `.com`, which is what the delegation wrote there.

prompt: The shop's servers must find `db.shop.internal`, and nobody outside may. One more VPC, in the `shop-staging` account, needs the same names. What does the lesson give for that?
hint: A private zone can be seen from more than one network.

choices.text: A second public zone, delegated only to staging
choices.why: A public zone is answered to anybody who asks; delegation cannot pick the asker.

choices.text: A copy of the private zone in the staging account, kept in step by hand
choices.why: It would work until the day the copies differ. The lesson names a way to share the one zone.

choices.text: Associate the same private zone with the staging VPC
choices.why: Right. `associate-vpc-with-hosted-zone` accepts a VPC in another account once the zone's owner has authorised it.

choices.text: A geolocation record that answers only for `10.30.0.0/16`
choices.why: Geolocation works on countries and continents, and a private range is in none of them.
